# Spreadsheet basics and functions {#sec-spreadsheet}

Any spreadsheet program works for this course. This appendix lists what you need, and where the programs differ.

## Operators

| Operation | Spreadsheet | R | Python |
|----------------------|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| Add, subtract        | `+ -`  | `+ -`  | `+ -`  |
| Multiply, divide     | `* /`  | `* /`  | `* /`  |
| Power                | `^`    | `^`    | `**`   |
| Text join            | `&`    | `paste()` | `+` |

Every spreadsheet formula starts with `=`.

## Cell references

| Written | Name | When filled down or across |
|---------|------|------------------------------|
| `B2`    | Relative reference | Row and column change |
| `$B$2`  | Absolute reference | Nothing changes |
| `B$2`, `$B2` | Mixed reference | Only the part without `$` changes |

## Decimal comma and list separator

Spreadsheets follow your computer's language settings. With German (or many other European) settings, numbers use a **decimal comma** (`0,19`) and the arguments of a function are separated by a **semicolon**: `=ROUND(B2;2)` instead of `=ROUND(B2,2)`. Function names may also be translated: in German Excel, `ROUND` is `RUNDEN`. This book uses English names, decimal points and commas between arguments.

## Functions used in this book

| Purpose | Excel | LibreOffice Calc | Google Sheets |
|------------------------|-------------------|------------------|----------------|
| Round to 2 decimals    | `=ROUND(B2,2)`    | same             | same |
| Square root            | `=SQRT(B2)`       | same             | same |
| Power (same as `^`)    | `=POWER(B2,3)`    | same             | same |
| Sum of a range         | `=SUM(B2:B4)`     | same             | same |
| Natural logarithm      | `=LN(B2)`         | same             | same |
| Logarithm to base 10   | `=LOG10(B2)` or `=LOG(B2)` | same    | same |
| Logarithm to any base  | `=LOG(B2,2)`      | same             | same |

`LOG` without a second argument uses base 10, unlike `log()` in R and Python, which is the natural logarithm.

## Goal seek (Session 2)

Goal seek changes one input cell until a formula cell reaches a target value.

| Program | Where to find it |
|------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Excel            | Data > What-If Analysis > Goal Seek (German: *Daten > Was-wäre-wenn-Analyse > Zielwertsuche*) |
| LibreOffice Calc | Tools > Goal Seek (German: *Extras > Zielwertsuche*) |
| Google Sheets    | No built-in goal seek; type the solved formula instead |

## Charts of a function (Session 3)

Put the inputs in one column and the formula results in the next, then select both columns.

| Program | How |
|------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Excel            | Insert > Charts > Scatter (with straight lines) |
| LibreOffice Calc | Insert > Chart > XY (Scatter), lines only |
| Google Sheets    | Insert > Chart, line chart, tick *Use column A as labels* |

## Money over time (Session 4)

These functions work the same way in Excel, LibreOffice Calc and Google Sheets. The rate is per period (monthly rate for monthly payments), and they follow a **sign convention**: money you receive is positive, money you pay is negative. That is why the examples put a minus sign in front of the amount you pay or borrow.

| Purpose | Function | German Excel | Example | Result |
|------------------------|-------------------|--------------|----------------------|----------|
| Loan instalment | `PMT(rate, nper, pv)` | `RMZ` | `=PMT(5%,4,-12000)` | 3,384.14 |
| Final value of a savings plan | `FV(rate, nper, pmt)` | `ZW` | `=FV(3%,5,-1000)` | 5,309.14 |
| Present value | `PV(rate, nper, pmt, fv)` | `BW` | `=PV(4%,5,0,-10000)` | 8,219.27 |
| Net present value | `NPV(rate, values)` | `NBW` | `=-12000+NPV(5%,B5:B8)` | (see @sec-present-value) |
| Internal rate of return | `IRR(values)` | `IKV` | `=IRR(B4:B8)` | 11.6 % |
| Number of periods | `NPER(rate, pmt, pv)` | `ZZR` | `=NPER(5%,-1500,10000)` | 8.31 |
| Interest rate | `RATE(nper, pmt, pv)` | `ZINS` | `=RATE(4,-3384.14,12000)` | 5 % |
| Effective annual rate | `EFFECT(rate, m)` | `EFFEKTIV` | `=EFFECT(6%,12)` | 6.17 % |
| Straight-line depreciation | `SLN(cost, salvage, life)` | `LIA` | `=SLN(12000,0,5)` | 2,400 |

`NPV` discounts the **first** value in its range by one period, so leave the investment of year 0 out of the range and add it separately.

For an investment, `IRR` finds the rate at which the NPV is zero; you can also find it with goal seek on the NPV cell.
